findings.headline: Annual scheme review confirms effective operation with no changes required for 2027/28
findings.detail: Review of the scheme's operation since April 2025 finds it working well. Paper states no significant issues have been identified. The scheme continues to support approximately 3,200 working-age households and 72.3% of those are disabled. No welfare policy announcements require scheme changes. Council meets statutory deadline to approve by 11 March 2027.
findings.matters: Confirmation that a service supporting vulnerable households is operating as intended with no emerging operational, cost or scope issues. Validates changes made in 2025 and signals service stability for the coming year.
findings.figures: 3,205 working-age households supported. 72.3 per cent are disabled. Approval deadline: 11 March 2027.
findings.quote: A review of the operation of the current scheme, which was introduced on 1 April 2025, has shown that the scheme is operating well and this report proposes no changes to the scheme in use this year.

findings.headline: Universal Credit migration to completion with 98 per cent take-up and 80 per cent of processing changes automated
findings.detail: Managed migration of Council Tax Reduction claimants to Universal Credit has completed. Of 3,205 working-age claimants, 3,133 (97.8%) now receive UC. Electronic DWP notifications and income tolerance measures have automated approximately 80% of administrative changes, reducing manual processing burden. This marks successful completion of a major system transition.
findings.matters: System migrations between welfare regimes create operational risk. Full completion with high automation signals the council has embedded the change and that administrative burden is now stable and manageable.
findings.figures: 3,133 of 3,205 working-age claimants (97.8%) on Universal Credit. 80 per cent of changes processed automatically.
findings.quote: The total number of CTR customers in receipt of Universal Credit has increased significantly as managed migration has reached completion. Of the 3,205 working age claimants 3,133 are in receipt of Universal Credit.

findings.headline: Council Tax Reduction expenditure increased 11 per cent between 2024/25 and 2026/27, driven by Council Tax rises rather than caseload growth
findings.detail: Total CTR costs rose from £6.65m to £7.38m forecast. Broadland's proportionate share (6%) increased from £399,000 to £442,800. The paper states costs rose because "Council Tax increases year on year", not because of growing reliance on support. Working-age caseload remained stable at 3,205 households across the period. Disabled households form 72.3% of the caseload.
findings.matters: Finance directors track welfare support costs as a proxy for community financial stress. Here, rising costs reflect inflation in the tax base rather than worsening hardship, indicating stable community circumstances despite inflationary pressure.
findings.quote: The increase in spend is primarily due to rising Council Tax charges rather than growth in caseload, as caseloads remain at similar levels.

findings.headline: Low-priority internal audits will not be completed due to resource constraints and oversubscription
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit reported that low-priority audit items are not expected to be completed during 2026/27 due to resource constraints and oversubscription. These audits remain under quarterly review but are only likely to progress if capacity becomes available.
findings.matters: This represents a gap in governance coverage that could delay identification of control issues or emerging risks
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit advised that these audits were not expected to be completed due to resource constraints and oversubscription

findings.headline: Finance team resourcing concerns to be addressed through graduate-level CIPFA apprentice recruitment, though recruitment not yet undertaken
findings.detail: Following committee concerns about staffing levels, the council has set aside funding for an apprenticeship and plans to recruit a graduate-level CIPFA apprentice to address workload pressures and support succession planning, but recruitment had not yet taken place.
findings.matters: Peer councils facing similar resourcing pressures want to understand how others are addressing this; lenders care about continuity in finance leadership and timely implementation of staffing solutions
findings.quote: funding had been set aside for the appointment of an accountancy apprentice, with plans to recruit a graduate-level CIPFA apprentice which will help with workload pressures and also be part of future succession planning; however, recruitment had not yet taken place.

findings.headline: Council failed to provide recharge information by backstop date, preventing auditors from completing testing
findings.detail: The council's finance team did not provide required recharge information by the deadline, which prevented external auditors (EY) from completing their testing within the available timeframe during the annual audit cycle.
findings.matters: The delay indicates potential process or resourcing issues in the finance function that affect audit quality and timeliness, signalling possible weaknesses in financial controls or record-keeping
findings.quote: In response to a query regarding issues with recharges, the Assistant Director of Finance confirmed that the required information had not been provided ahead of the backstop date, resulting in EY being unable to complete the testing within the available timeframe.

findings.headline: Sale of Thorpe Lodge agreed subject to planning; council remains liable for building damage until completion
findings.detail: Broadland has agreed to sell Thorpe Lodge but remains responsible for the building's condition until sale completion, with an 18-month long stop date. The site has been vacated with limited insurance cover and has experienced break-in attempts. The listed building elements and potential financial and reputational impact led to addition to the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.matters: The council faces a contingent liability for an asset at risk of deterioration with limited insurance protection during the sale process, affecting its balance sheet risk position
findings.figures: 18-month long stop date
findings.quote: She explained that the Council remained responsible for the condition of the building until completion of sale. Members noted the potential for damage of the building, including risks arising from attempted break-ins, weather-related impacts and limitations in insurance cover since the site was vacated. It was explained that the risk had been placed on the SRR due to the potential scale of financial and reputational impact, particularly in relation to the listed elements of the building

findings.headline: Council rejected option to increase maximum CTR support from 87% to 100% of eligible Council Tax charge
findings.detail: The annual review considered increasing support to provide greater help to residents on severely low incomes but decided the cost increase was not justified. The 87% level was retained as providing an effective balance between supporting residents and managing cost while supporting Council Tax collection.
findings.matters: Shows how a council assesses the cost-benefit of expanding support; demonstrates active management of the tension between supporting vulnerable residents and financial sustainability
findings.figures: Current support level: 87%; rejected option: 100%
findings.quote: An option would be to increase the maximum level of support from 87% to 100%. This would provide greater help to residents on severely low incomes but would increase the cost to the Council.

findings.headline: Council Tax Reduction support costs rose from £6.65m (2024/25) to £7.38m (2026/27), with Broadland's 6% share increasing from £399,000 to £442,800
findings.detail: The increase is driven by rising Council Tax charges year-on-year rather than growth in caseloads, which remained stable at approximately 3,200 working-age households. The paper confirms the scheme is being operated sustainably within existing staff resources.
findings.matters: Growing support costs from external drivers are a predictable financial pressure that peer councils also face; shows how one council is managing sustainable cost growth
findings.figures: Total CTR cost: £6.65m (2024/25), £7.06m (2025/26), £7.38m (2026/27 forecast); Broadland 6% share: £399,000, £423,600, £442,800; working-age caseload: 3,205 households
findings.quote: Since 2024/25, CTR assessments have increased because Council Tax increases year on year, which was predicted. The total Council Tax Liability forgone for CTR totalled: 2024/25 £6.65m, 2025/26 £7.06m, 2026/27* £7.38m

findings.committee: Broadland Communities, Housing and Planning Policy Development Panel
findings.headline: Council has created operational dependency on automated Universal Credit data feeds with no documented fallback if systems become unavailable
findings.detail: Section 6.1 identifies a risk that if UC data automation fails or becomes unavailable, manual processing would be required, increasing workloads and potentially causing delays in assessments and Council Tax billing. With 80% of routine changes now automated, the council is dependent on continuity of DWP data without a documented contingency plan.
findings.matters: System outages affecting DWP data feeds would create processing delays and potentially disrupt Council Tax billing cycles. The council has moved to an architecture dependent on continuous external data feed availability.
findings.figures: Approximately 80% of changes processed automatically via UC/DWP data.
findings.quote: if the automation fails or is unavailable, claims and changes would need to be processed manually, increasing workloads and potentially causing delays in assessments and updates to Council Tax bills.

findings.committee: Broadland Communities, Housing and Planning Policy Development Panel
findings.headline: Universal Credit managed migration completed, with 3,133 of 3,205 working-age CTR claimants now receiving UC and approximately 80% of changes processed automatically
findings.detail: Broadland has successfully transitioned its CTR caseload to UC. Electronic DWP notifications provide real-time income updates; an income tolerance introduced April 2025 reduces unnecessary recalculations and provides stability for residents. Approximately 80% of changes are now processed automatically. The council administers this through 26.19 FTE in the Benefits team, with CTR work estimated at approximately 17% of their time.
findings.matters: Other councils managing UC migration can see this approach works and can be delivered within current staffing. Demonstrates successful handling of the largest welfare transition in recent years with automation supporting efficiency.
findings.figures: 3,133 of 3,205 working-age claimants on UC; approximately 80% of changes automatic; 26.19 FTE Benefits team; approximately 17% of time on working-age CTR.
findings.quote: Of the 3,205 working age claimants 3,133 are in receipt of Universal Credit.

findings.committee: Broadland Communities, Housing and Planning Policy Development Panel
findings.headline: Council examined reducing working-age support from 87% but concluded the saving would be offset by increased Council Tax collection losses
findings.detail: The council considered but rejected reducing support, noting that many residents on low incomes would be unable to pay higher bills and would default. With 98–99% of working-age CTR claimants receiving Universal Credit, cutting support would likely create arrears, higher recovery and enforcement costs, potentially offsetting any financial saving. The council concluded the current 87% level 'supports Council Tax collection and helps avoid costly recovery action.'
findings.matters: Peer councils facing budget pressure would value this analysis—evidence that cutting welfare support backfires on collection. Shows the council has modeled the trade-off and rejected cost reduction on financial grounds.
findings.figures: 98–99% of working-age CTR caseload receive Universal Credit; 3,205 working-age households; 3,133 on UC; maximum support at 87% of eligible Council Tax charge.
findings.quote: Reducing support from 87% may appear to save money, but many of these residents would be unable to pay the additional Council Tax, so the Council would be unlikely to collect the full amount.

findings.committee: Broadland Communities, Housing and Planning Policy Development Panel
findings.headline: Council Tax Reduction spend rose from £6.65m in 2024/25 to £7.38m in 2026/27, with increases driven by rising Council Tax charges rather than caseload growth
findings.detail: Working-age CTR caseload has remained flat to declining over 2024–2026 (ranging from 3,199 to 3,317), yet total spend grew 11% over three years. Broadland's 6% share increased from £399,000 to £442,800. The council attributes this entirely to Council Tax rises pushing up the support amount per claimant, not to increased demand.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand that CTR obligations grow automatically with Council Tax rises, independent of demand. This affects multi-year budget forecasting and revenue planning.
findings.quote: The increase in spend is primarily due to rising Council Tax charges rather than growth in caseload, as caseloads remain at similar levels.

findings.headline: Council identifies that reducing Council Tax Reduction support could increase collection losses and enforcement costs, offsetting anticipated savings.
findings.detail: The paper notes that 98-99 per cent of working-age CTR recipients receive Universal Credit (extremely vulnerable population). Section 6.5 explicitly states that reducing CTR support 'may not generate an equivalent increase in collectable Council Tax income and may instead increase hardship, debt and recovery costs'. This reveals a direct economic link between welfare support and tax collection effectiveness.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand that council tax collection depends on welfare support infrastructure; reductions could worsen net financial position through arrears and enforcement costs.
findings.figures: 98-99 per cent of working-age claimants on Universal Credit
findings.quote: Any reduction or removal of working-age CTR support would need to be considered carefully to ensure there is not an adverse impact on Council Tax collection.

findings.headline: SNC's share of Council Tax Reduction costs has grown 11 per cent over two years, from £541,100 to £601,300, as council tax levels rise.
findings.detail: The council's share of total CTR costs grew from £541,100 in 2024/25 to £577,500 in 2025/26 to £601,300 in 2026/27. The paper notes caseloads remain stable; the growth is entirely driven by council tax rises year-on-year. The pattern is expected to continue as council tax increases.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand the council's growing welfare commitments and how they scale with council tax increases, affecting budget sustainability.
findings.figures: £541,100 (2024/25), £577,500 (2025/26), £601,300 (2026/27); approximately 11 per cent growth over two years
findings.quote: The increase in spend is primarily due to rising Council Tax charges rather than growth in caseload, as caseloads remain at similar levels.

findings.paper_title: 260730 REP Annual Governance Statement APP A
findings.headline: Broadland Growth Limited now wholly council-owned with no active development sites following NORSE withdrawal
findings.detail: NORSE withdrew from joint ownership of Broadland Growth Limited on 31 March 2025, making the company wholly owned by the council. The company has completed two developments historically but currently operates no live sites. Unclear what financial exposure or asset write-down this represents.
findings.matters: Changes in company ownership structure and project activity can indicate financial exposure or asset impairment risks that affect council balance sheet
findings.figures: 31 March 2025 NORSE withdrawal; two developments delivered to date; currently no live sites
findings.quote: Broadland Growth Limited was a jointly owned company with NORSE. However, on 31 March 2025 Norse withdrew so that Broadland Growth Limited is now a wholly owned company. The company has delivered two developments to date. However currently, the company has no live sites.

findings.paper_title: 260730 REP Annual Governance Statement APP A
findings.headline: No formal governance review yet undertaken for council-owned and associated companies
findings.detail: The council has not conducted a formal review of client-side governance arrangements for Broadland Living Ltd and its involvement in Norfolk Environmental Credits Ltd joint venture. An internal audit review is scheduled for 2026/27 to assess whether roles, responsibilities and reporting mechanisms remain fit for purpose.
findings.matters: Lack of periodic formal review of company governance creates risk that oversight and accountability mechanisms may not adequately protect council interests or manage company exposures
findings.figures: Review planned 2026/27
findings.quote: A formal review of the Council's client-side governance arrangements for its companies has not yet been undertaken. Given the importance of effective oversight, transparency and risk management in relation to Council-owned or associated companies, it is important that these arrangements are periodically reviewed to ensure roles, responsibilities and reporting mechanisms remain clear, robust and fit for purpose.

findings.paper_title: 260730 REP Annual Governance Statement APP A
findings.headline: Internal audit recommendations not consistently implemented within agreed timelines
findings.detail: Managers reported that audit recommendations were not always implemented on time. While Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer oversight produced in-year improvements, the issue remains flagged for continued monitoring through 2026/27. This indicates control weaknesses are not being resolved promptly.
findings.matters: Delayed fixes to identified control weaknesses mean governance gaps persist longer than planned, delaying mitigation of identified risks
findings.figures: Ongoing monitoring through 2026/27
findings.quote: Some managers highlighted this is an area whereby recommendations were not always implemented in line with the agreed timeline. This is something that the Section 151 Officer and Monitoring Officer have kept a close eye on and in year improvements have been realised. This will continue to be monitored.

findings.paper_title: 260730 REP Annual Governance Statement APP A
findings.headline: 2024/25 financial accounts received disclaimed audit opinions due to external auditor resource constraints
findings.detail: Ernst & Young was unable to complete audit procedures to sufficient standard before statutory deadlines. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not express an opinion on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. This prevents verification of the council's 2024/25 financial position.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audited accounts to assess financial position and creditworthiness; disclaimed opinions mean statements cannot be verified and confidence in reported figures is undermined
findings.figures: 2024/25 Accounts; disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: Like many local authorities affected by the national backlog of local authority external audits, these Accounts received disclaimed opinions as EY did not have the required resources available to complete all the detailed audit procedures that would be needed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to issue an unmodified audit opinion before the statutory backstop dates.

findings.headline: Council has internally borrowed £1.117m to fund temporary accommodation with planned external refinancing contingent on interest rate falls.
findings.detail: The council borrowed £468,000 in 2024/25 and £1.117m in 2025/26 internally to fund temporary accommodation under the Local Authority Housing Fund. It plans to refinance this externally through PWLB borrowing only when interest rates fall sufficiently to ensure rental income covers interest costs.
findings.matters: Shows the council is funding temporary accommodation expansion using internal reserves with uncertain external refinancing. The plan depends on both rate falls and rental income adequacy, creating timing risk.
findings.figures: £1.117m borrowed in 2025/26, total CFR £1,654k, Bank Rate 3.75%, 10-year PWLB 5.50%
findings.quote: The Council internally borrowed £468,000 in 2024/25 and £1.117m in 2025/26 to fund LAHF temporary accommodation. External borrowing will be undertaken for this sum as and when interest rates fall sufficiently, to ensure that the rental income fully covers the interest cost.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Business rates collection is below target at 95.9%, though one timing issue accounts for much of the shortfall.
findings.detail: In-year collection rate is 95.9% against a target of 98%. The council explains that one large property on Broadland Business Park (£552,225 charge) did not appear on the rating list until 25 March 2026, so collection was impossible in-year. Excluding this property, the rate would have been 97.38%, an improvement on the prior year (97.06%). Cash collected was £34m vs £31m the prior year. The council flags economic pressure: 'The economic climate continues to put pressure on business incomes which will impact on collection rates.'
findings.matters: Below-target collection rates are a leading indicator of business stress on the ground; even with a one-off explanation, the underlying economic headwind is noted by the council itself.
findings.figures: Collection rate 95.9% vs target 98%; cash collected £34m (up from £31m in prior year); one property account for ~£552k shortfall
findings.quote: However, there was one large property on the Broadland Business Park which did not come into our rating list until 25 March 2026, and we were therefore unable to collect the £552,225 25/26 charge before the end of Q4.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Apprenticeship levy balance reduced to £20,045; further commitments risk requiring 25% employer contribution from autumn 2026
findings.detail: The council notes that 'Apprenticeship levy spend during Q3 continues to exceed monthly levy income, reducing the overall balance to £20,045.' The risk notes that any additional apprenticeships beyond current commitments may require a 25% employer contribution, since the levy funds will be insufficient. This is a cash-flow risk on a specific training commitment.
findings.matters: A dwindling balance in a restricted fund suggests the council is drawing down reserves on operational commitments; it also signals potential breaks in apprenticeship provision if funding does not recover.
findings.figures: Apprenticeship levy balance: £20,045; anticipated funding changes in Autumn 2026
findings.quote: Apprenticeship levy spend during Q3 continues to exceed monthly levy income, reducing the overall balance to £20,045 and mitigating the risk of funds expiring.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Affordable housing delivery has slowed significantly; from 289 units in 2024/25 to 183 in 2025/26.
findings.detail: While 183 units exceeded the annual target of 95, this represents a material slowdown: 289 were delivered the prior year. The council attributes this to 'completion of several large development sites and a reduced number of new sites commencing construction.' The housing register has 984 applicants, and applicants in temporary accommodation cannot access affordable-home-ownership products, limiting move-on options.
findings.matters: Slowing affordable housing delivery is a leading indicator of sector stress (sites finishing, no pipeline) and directly impacts the council's ability to reduce TA costs by moving residents on; it also signals planning and development risk.
findings.figures: 183 affordable homes delivered in 2025/26 vs 289 in 2024/25; housing register 984 households
findings.quote: A slowdown in new affordable housing delivery is emerging across the district. This reflects the completion of several large development sites and a reduced number of new sites commencing construction.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is creating organizational uncertainty and a specific risk of staff disengagement.
findings.detail: The council's staff satisfaction survey has been extended to include 'staff sentiment around Local Government Reorganisation.' The risk register flags: 'Due to the recent LGR announcement there may be apathy amongst the workforce culminating in reduced response rates.' An LGR reserve has been created to fund additional resources for reorganisation. This risk spans both organizational readiness and retention.
findings.matters: LGR creates both known costs (the reserve) and hidden ones (productivity loss, turnover, knowledge drain during transition); staff apathy during a reorganisation is hard to manage and often precedes attrition.
findings.figures: LGR reserve created; staff turnover at 16% (target 15%)
findings.quote: Due to the recent LGR announcement there maybe apathy amongst the workforce culminating in reduced response rates which will ultimately provide less data to work with and respond to.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Four strategic risks are assessed as above the council's risk appetite, including housing pressure and LGR reorganisation.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'There are four risks with residual risk above the Council's risk appetite.' These include BDCM2 (Local Government Reorganisation and delivery), BDCM3 (failure to achieve efficiency savings through collaboration), BDCSI3 (housing pressure), and BDCM7 (Thorpe Lodge deterioration). For each, the council either proposes controls to bring them within appetite or recommends accepting them at current risk levels.
findings.matters: A council identifying multiple risks above its own risk appetite indicates governance stress; the fact that some risks are being *accepted* rather than controlled suggests difficult tradeoffs between cost and mitigation.
findings.figures: Four strategic risks above council risk appetite identified in Q4 report
findings.quote: There are four risks with residual risk above the Council's risk appetite. All have proposed controls to bring them within the Council's risk appetite or a recommendation to accept them at the current level of controlled risk.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Business support grant funding has been cut by nearly half, reducing the council's ability to support local enterprise.
findings.detail: Grant funding available for Business Builder dropped from £558,000 in 2024/25 to £301,000 in 2025/26. Businesses supported fell to 86 against a target of 124; jobs created/supported were 46 against a target of 55. The council flags risk around future funding: UKSPF and REPF programmes are concluding, creating uncertainty about successor funding and the future structure of local business support.
findings.matters: A sharp reduction in discretionary spend signals budget stress; the council's inability to set targets proportionate to available resources suggests reactive rather than proactive budget management, and uncertainty about future funding reduces visibility.
findings.figures: Grant funding reduced from £558,000 to £301,000 (46% reduction); 86 businesses supported vs target 124; 46 jobs created/supported vs target 55
findings.quote: Delivery during the year reflected a reduction in available grant funding, which reduced from £558,000 in 2024/25 to £301,000 in 2025/26. With UK Shared Prosperity Fund and Rural England Prosperity Fund programmes concluding, there is uncertainty around the availability of successor funding streams.

findings.paper_title: 260609 REP Performance and Risk Cabinet Report Quarter 4
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are rising as demand grows and spot-purchase placements become necessary.
findings.detail: Households in temporary accommodation reached 110 by year-end, with 35 families and children in spot-purchased or council-owned TA. The council notes that spot-purchase accommodation is significantly more expensive than owned stock. Housing pressure (BDCSI3) is identified as a strategic risk with residual rating above the council's risk appetite.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled growth in TA costs is a major budget pressure for councils; spot-purchase rates typically exceed owned-stock running costs by 30–50%, and growing numbers of complex-needs residents (those difficult to prevent or rehouse) are extending stays.
findings.figures: 110 households in TA by Q4; 35 households with children in temporary accommodation; housing register at 984 households
findings.quote: Increases in demand for TA or increases in the time spent in TA will put financial pressure on council budgets due to the need to use more spot purchase accommodation which is more expensive than owned TA.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: 44% of total investments concentrated in wholly owned property companies; different risk profile from financial institution holdings
findings.detail: Of £85.04m total investments, £37.715m (44%) are loans and equity in Big Sky property companies. These have different risk characteristics. The council's other investments are with A- rated counterparties. Property/commercial assets are exposed to real estate market cycles.
findings.matters: Significant concentration in non-financial-institution assets means the council's investment returns and potential capital losses are exposed to property market performance, not just financial market spreads.
findings.figures: Total investments £85.040m. Shareholding BSV £6.468m. Loans to BSPM £4.987m. Loans to BSD £26.260m. Total Big Sky £37.715m (44% of total).
findings.quote: Investments totalled £85.040 million as at 31 March 2026. This includes: treasury loans of £47.3 million loans and equity in the Council's wholly owned companies of £37.715 million.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: Investment income materially dependent on wholly owned company performance; Big Sky Development income outperformed budget by 37%
findings.detail: Interest received from core external investments was £2.321m vs budget £1.825m (+27%). But critically, Big Sky Development income alone was £1.652m vs budget £1.201m, an outperformance of £451k (37%). This represents 40% of total interest income. The council's investment income is significantly exposed to the performance of its property companies.
findings.matters: A material portion of budgeted revenue income is dependent on commercial property company performance. Downturn in company returns or property market would directly impact the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Total interest position £4.172m vs budget £3.225m. Big Sky Development £1.652m vs budget £1.201m (variance £451k). Proportion from Big Sky £1.85m of £4.17m total (44%).
findings.quote: Core interest earned was £2,321,000, which was £496,000 over budget. Investment Income – Big Sky Development 1,201 [budget] 1,652 [actual] 451 [variance].

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: External borrowing stands at operational boundary, leaving limited headroom for new capital projects
findings.detail: External borrowing is £24.5m against an operational boundary of £25m (98% utilised). All existing borrowing matures in 10+ years, but the tight boundary constrains the council's ability to take on new borrowing without revising prudential indicators.
findings.matters: Limits the council's financial flexibility. Any new capital programme requiring external borrowing would need approval to raise the operational boundary.
findings.figures: External borrowing £24.5m. Operational boundary £25m. Authorised limit £30m.
findings.quote: Prudential Indicator for Affordability 4 – External Debt Authorised (Max) Limit £30m Operational Boundary £25m Yes Current external borrowing £24.5m.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: Big Sky Developments loans increased 35% to £26.26m; St Giles Park project financing was restructured through external refinancing
findings.detail: Loans to Big Sky Developments Limited increased from £19.46m at March 2025 to £26.26m at March 2026. During the year (8 July 2025), the council novated its St Giles Park project loans into a new credit facility, presumably with an external lender. The council continued to provide capital to the company after this refinancing.
findings.matters: Shows significant ongoing capital deployment by the council through its property companies, with material refinancing activity during the year. Suggests the council is bearing development risk on major projects.
findings.figures: Loans to BSD increased £6.8m (35%). Loans and equity in Big Sky companies total £37.715m at 31 March 2026.
findings.quote: The Council also had outstanding loans, shown in the table above, as at 31 March 2026 to Big Sky Developments Limited (BSD). The loans with Big Sky Developments Limited for St Giles Park were novated into a new credit facility from 8th July 2025.

findings.headline: Broadland Living Limited restructured into single loan agreement in November 2025
findings.detail: The council consolidated two previous loan agreements with its wholly-owned company BLL into a single new agreement in November 2025. The restructured arrangement includes £1.161m at 4% interest and a new £774k at 0% loan (equivalent to government grant funding received). The shift from two agreements to one, and the introduction of grant-funded borrowing, suggests the previous structure required financial restructuring.
findings.matters: Company financing was materially restructured mid-year; grant funding is being deployed as a 0% loan rather than used to reduce capital requirement
findings.figures: Loans to BLL: £1.161m at 4% + £774k at 0% (grant equivalent); shareholding £50k
findings.quote: In November 2025, a new loan agreement was agreed with Broadland Living Limited replacing the previous two agreements.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing for temporary accommodation growing; external borrowing deferred pending rate falls
findings.detail: The council internally borrowed £468,000 in 2024/25 and £1.117m in 2025/26 for LAHF temporary accommodation, now totalling £1.585m in the Capital Financing Requirement. The council plans to externalize this debt 'as and when interest rates fall sufficiently, to ensure that the rental income fully covers the interest cost'. This defers borrowing cost exposure but assumes rate falls; the treasury advisor's April 2026 forecast shows bank rate staying at 3.75% through most of 2026.
findings.matters: Material capital commitment (£1.585m) currently unfunded by external debt; borrowing plan depends on rate falls that treasury advisors do not forecast
findings.figures: Internal borrowing: £468k (2024/25) + £1.117m (2025/26) = £1.585m total; CFR £1.654m; bank rate forecast 3.75% Jun-Dec 2026
findings.quote: The Council internally borrowed £468,000 in 2024/25 and £1.117m in 2025/26 to fund LAHF temporary accommodation. External borrowing will be undertaken for this sum as and when interest rates fall sufficiently, to ensure that the rental income fully covers the interest cost.

findings.headline: Nutrient Mitigation Fund £14.25m loan book depends on nutrient credit market sales
findings.detail: The council has loaned £14.25m of a £20.19m total fund, with major portions contingent on market conditions. Bid 29 (£9m) and Bid 33 (£5m) have repayment schedules based on 'value of relevant credit sales' rather than fixed terms, with long-stop dates between 2029 and 2033. If the nascent nutrient credit market does not deliver expected demand from housebuilders seeking planning consent, repayments will be delayed or impaired.
findings.matters: Material contingent asset (22% of council investments) where repayment depends on market development in a regulatory framework less than four years old; impairment could affect reserves
findings.figures: £14.250m outstanding of £20.194m loaned; Bid 29 £9m (long-stop 31 Mar 29), Bid 33 £5m (long-stop 2033)
findings.quote: Based on value of relevant credit sales, with a long stop date of 31 Dec 29

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: Gilt yields spiked to 5.00% and borrowing costs have risen materially, with rate cuts limited
findings.detail: 10-year Gilt yields reached 5.00% in late March 2026 driven by Middle East conflict. Bank Rate remains at 3.75% with minimal cuts expected for remainder of 2026 due to persistent inflation at 3.8% and tight labour markets. Borrowing is significantly more expensive than earlier in the year.
findings.matters: Future borrowing costs have risen sharply; if the council needs additional capital borrowing, it will pay materially higher interest rates than historical norms, affecting scheme affordability.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB Gilt yields 5.00% (late March); Bank Rate 3.75%; CPI inflation peaked at 3.8%
findings.quote: Moreover, borrowing has become more expensive in 2025/26. Gilt yield have risen materially in March 2026, more than reversing the falls earlier in the financial year.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: External borrowing of £24.5m leaves only £0.5m headroom against operational boundary of £25m
findings.detail: The council has total external borrowing of £24.5m (£20m borrowed March 2022 for capital programme; £4.5m borrowed May 2025 for Long Stratton by-pass) against an operational boundary of £25m. This minimal headroom limits flexibility for additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Limited headroom means the council is approaching its self-imposed borrowing ceiling and will need to rely on internal resources or service cuts to fund new capital projects.
findings.figures: Current external borrowing £24.5m vs operational boundary £25m (£0.5m headroom); authorised maximum £30m
findings.quote: The Council borrowed £20m on 15 March 2022 in order to help fund its capital programme. And In May 2025 £4.5m was borrowed as part of the financing arrangements for the Long Stratton by-pass.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: Investment income exceeded budget by £947,000, with Big Sky Development overperforming by £451,000
findings.detail: Total investment income was £4,172,000 against a budget of £3,225,000. Big Sky Development contributed £1,652,000 against a budget of £1,201,000, suggesting stronger-than-expected property portfolio returns. Core general investment income also outperformed by £496,000.
findings.matters: Material overperformance raises questions about budget conservatism; lenders need to understand if property returns are sustainable or one-off, as this underpins the council's cash position.
findings.figures: Total variance £947,000; Big Sky Development variance £451,000; core investment income £2,321,000 vs budget £1,825,000
findings.quote: The Council's budgeted core investment income for the year was set at £1,825,000. Core interest earned was £2,321,000, which was £496,000 over budget.

findings.paper_title: SNC Treasury Management Annual Review Report 202526 V1
findings.headline: Loans to Big Sky Developments Limited increased by £6.8m to £26.26m, refinanced into a new facility
findings.detail: The council's lending to Big Sky Developments Limited grew significantly from £19.46m at 31 March 2025 to £26.26m at 31 March 2026. The loans for St Giles Park were novated into a new credit facility from 8 July 2025, indicating substantial refinancing of a major development project.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand concentration risk in the council's portfolio and whether exposure to subsidiary property developments is growing faster than it can service.
findings.figures: Loans to BSD increased from £19,460,000 to £26,260,000 (£6.8m increase in one year)
findings.quote: The loans with Big Sky Developments Limited for St Giles Park were novated into a new credit facility from 8th July 2025.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates structural uncertainty; projects selected for pre-reorganisation delivery
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that local government reorganisation and devolution plans would require the capital programme to be reviewed. Capital projects for 2026/27-2027/28 were specifically selected to have high likelihood of delivery 'before LGR takes place', indicating uncertainty about the council's continued existence in its current form.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty about the council's future affects the reliability of multi-year financial projections; reorganisation could alter service delivery, debt obligations, and financial sustainability
findings.figures: Capital years 2028/29-2030/31 face delivery uncertainty if LGR proceeds
findings.quote: If plans for devolution and local government reorganisation progress then the capital programme will need to be reviewed in light of any decisions taken.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Council's main buildings identified as major 20-year liability but condition surveys not yet commissioned
findings.detail: The Capital Strategy identifies main council buildings as the greatest ongoing capital liability over the next 20 years but states the council has not yet commissioned condition surveys to determine actual maintenance and upgrading needs, leaving the financial scope of required building investment unquantified.
findings.matters: Unquantified building condition assessments represent a material gap in capital planning; actual maintenance costs could exceed current projections and force future reserve depletion or additional borrowing
findings.figures: 20-year liability unquantified; no condition surveys completed
findings.quote: The main council buildings are likely to present the greatest ongoing capital liability for the Council over the next 20 years... In order to determine future liabilities, the Council will need to commission condition surveys for Council assets.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Council approves £1m borrowing for temporary accommodation property purchases
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £1,000,000 of external borrowing specifically for purchasing temporary accommodation properties in 2026/27. This is the only external borrowing in the five-year programme, indicating the council is using capital investment to respond to housing demand.
findings.matters: New borrowing commitment affects the council's debt profile and utilisation of prudential borrowing headroom; temporary accommodation expansion signals ongoing housing demand pressures
findings.figures: £1,000,000 borrowing approved for 2026/27
findings.quote: Borrowing for temporary accommodation properties 1,000,000

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: General Reserve will fall 32% from £6.9m to £4.7m by 2030/31 as capital programme draws down reserves
findings.detail: The council plans to draw £3.839m from General Reserve across the five-year capital programme. The running balance on General Reserve declines from £6,902,910 in 2026/27 to £4,698,183 by 2030/31, with the largest drawdowns occurring in years 4 and 5.
findings.matters: A 32% reduction in financial reserves weakens the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls and reduces financial resilience
findings.figures: General Reserve running balance from £6.9m to £4.7m; £3.839m drawn over five years
findings.quote: Running balance on General Reserve 6,902,910 6,902,910 6,902,910 6,427,505 4,698,183

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: National pay settlement for 2026/27 not yet known; budget contingent on 3.5% cost of living rise that may be exceeded
findings.detail: The budget includes 3.5% pay inflation and incremental scale point increases. However, the result of national pay bargaining is not expected until spring 2026, after the budget is set. If the actual settlement exceeds 3.5%, the budget will be at risk. Pay costs represent 87% of gross service costs.
findings.matters: Largest cost area in the budget; actual pay outcome unknown at time of budget setting creates material contingent liability
findings.figures: Pay budget £13,653k of £15,482k gross cost of services (87%); 3.5% increase assumed
findings.quote: Furthermore, it is likely that we will not know the result of the national pay bargaining until spring 2026 (i.e. after the 2026/27 budget has been set).

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: Mixed Recycling Facility gate fees are variable and volatile; £1.14m budget estimate subject to significant variance
findings.detail: The budget allows £1.14m for MRF processing at £95/tonne (12,000 tonnes). However, the contract includes a variable gate fee that has 'fluctuated significantly in recent years', meaning actual costs could be materially different from the estimate. This is an uncontrolled cost risk.
findings.matters: Material uncontrolled cost exposure; waste gate fees depend on commodity markets outside council control
findings.figures: £1,140,000 budgeted; 12,000 tonnes @ £95/tonne
findings.quote: The budget includes an allowance for Mixed Recycling Facility (MRF) processing costs of £1,140,000 (12,000 tonnes at £95) which is the same as in 2025/26. However, given that the agreement is for a variable gate fee the actual costs will vary from this figure. The actual gate fee has fluctuated significantly in recent years, and thus there could be a material difference in MRF processing costs.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision by end of March 2026; structural uncertainty for next 1–2 years
findings.detail: The government requires all two-tier councils to develop reorganisation proposals. Broadland expects a 'minded to' decision by end of March 2026, with formal Structural Change Order in the autumn. The council is budgeting £60k for LGR costs and setting aside £1m in a new reserve, but full financial and structural impact is unknown.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation creates uncertainty about the council's continued existence and financial obligations; critical for lender risk assessment
findings.figures: £60,000 revenue budget; £1,000,000 transferred to LGR reserve in 2026/27
findings.quote: A 'minded to' decision is expected before the end of March 2026, with the formal Structural Change Order expected in the Autumn. However, if plans for devolution and LGR progress then the revenue budget and the medium-term financial projections will need to be reviewed and adjusted in light of any reorganisation decisions taken.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: EPR income falling from £1.925m to £1.552m, with payments from 2027 varying by council performance
findings.detail: EPR (packaging waste) income is falling from £1.925m to £1.552m. From 2027 onwards, payments will vary based on individual council Efficiency and Effectiveness performance, creating explicit risk of further reduction if Broadland scores below average.
findings.matters: Material income declining with structural risk of further cuts tied to government performance benchmarking
findings.quote: From 2027 individual local authority performance will be measured in relation to their Efficiency and Effectiveness, with the potential for the level of funding to be reduced if the performance is below average compared to similar authorities.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: Homelessness placements up 58% in 12 months; nightly booked costs up 28%
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation placements have grown from 66 (two years ago) to 76 (one year ago) to 104 (January 2026). The council has contained costs by purchasing 52 council-owned bedspaces, but the budget for nightly booked/B&B accommodation has had to increase materially to £1.04m, creating an uncontrolled cost risk if demand continues to accelerate.
findings.matters: Rapid demand growth for a highly expensive service; costs could escalate further if the council runs out of owned capacity
findings.quote: As at 1st January 2026 there were 104 BDC households being accommodated in temporary accommodation, this compares to 76 households a year ago and 66 households two years ago. If demand continues to increase as anticipated, and the Council has to place more families in more expensive nightly booked / B&B accommodation then the cost to the Council could increase significantly.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: Business rates pooling benefit of £600k also lost; Norfolk councils abandon pooling
findings.detail: Norfolk councils have decided not to participate in business rates pooling for 2026/27 because the reformed pooling mechanism offers limited upside benefit and material downside risk. This removes a £600k income source from 2025/26.
findings.matters: Another material income source removed; shows how changes to government funding architecture directly reduce council finances
findings.quote: In light of the limited upside benefit and downside risk it has been decided across Norfolk not to pool in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 260210 REP Revenue Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 (BDC)
findings.headline: Business rates growth benefit of £825k eliminated by government baseline reset
findings.detail: The council's historic business rates growth of £825k in 2025/26 is lost under the government's reset. All growth is remeasured from a new, lower baseline from April 2026, meaning historic accumulated growth no longer counts and must be rebuilt.
findings.matters: Removes a material income stream; demonstrates volatility in the rates system lenders depend on
findings.quote: However, due to resetting the baseline, this historic growth will no longer be relevant, and growth is reset to zero so that only new growth post 1 April 2026 will be within retention system. Consequently, no growth benefit has been budgeted for in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Structural funding headwind emerges from 2027/28 as temporary support ends
findings.detail: The baseline reduction is permanent but masked in 2026/27 by the grant. Once the grant expires, the council faces ongoing annual reductions as the lower baseline becomes the new normal, creating cumulative funding pressure in outer years.
findings.matters: The council's medium-term financial sustainability depends on managing these reductions through savings or service changes, signalling potential borrowing pressure or difficult decisions ahead
findings.figures: Core Spending Power projected down £54k in 2027/28 compared to provisional figures
findings.quote: And a lower baseline means less income is protected from funding cuts, so the General Government Grant line reduces by £562k in 2026/27, £95k in 2027/28 and £3k in 2028/29.

findings.headline: One-off Adjustment Support Grant masks structural funding reduction in 2026/27
findings.detail: The government provided a temporary £518k grant to offset the loss from baseline reduction. This is explicitly one-off, expiring after 2026/27. General Government Grant reduces by £562k in 2026/27, then a further £95k in 2027/28 and £3k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: The council's immediate budget is cushioned by temporary support, but this conceals a permanent structural reduction that will create funding pressure once the grant expires
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant £518k (2026/27 only); General Government Grant reductions of £562k (26/27), £95k (27/28), £3k (28/29)
findings.quote: However, the Government will provide a new one off 'Adjustment Support Grant' of £518k in 2026/27 to offset the loss in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline funding recalculated downward by £826k
findings.detail: The government reduced the assumed 2025/26 business rates baseline from £7.697m to £6.871m due to recalculating historical business rates pooling gains. This permanent reduction in baseline funding cascades through the council's funding settlement and creates a structural headwind.
findings.matters: A material downward restatement of the council's baseline funding position affects the underlying sustainability of its financial plan and reveals the council's funding base is weaker than previously assumed
findings.figures: Business rates baseline reduced from £7.697m to £6.871m
findings.quote: The Government has reduced the assumed 2025/26 business rates baseline funding level from £7.697m to £6.871m - by recalculating assumed historical business rates pooling gains.

findings.headline: Long-term investment restrictions implemented due to potential Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: Broadland has removed ability to invest in long-term Gilt-edged securities, Bonds, or Property Funds citing 'potential for LGR'. Principal sums invested for longer than one year are being sharply reduced from £3,000k (2025/26) to £2,000k (2026/27) to nil from 2027/28 onwards. The council explicitly states that given LGR potential 'it would be prudent to ensure investments are kept short term'.
findings.matters: Preemptive restriction of investment strategy signals material uncertainty about the council's future structure and independence, which affects long-term financial planning and could impact debt management under a successor entity.
findings.figures: Principal sums invested for longer than 1 year: £3,000k (2025/26), £2,000k (2026/27), nil (2027/28 onwards)
findings.quote: Given the potential of LGR it would be prudent to ensure investments are kept short term, hence these limits have been reduced compared to 2025/26. Appendix 3 - Removing the ability to invest in Long-Term Gilt-edged securities, Bonds, or Property Funds given the potential for LGR.

findings.headline: Investment income projected to fall 43% due to Bank Rate cuts and gilt yield pressure.
findings.detail: Broadland's investment returns are forecast to decline from £1,914,000 in 2025/26 to £1,100,000 in 2026/27. This is driven by falling interest rates: Bank Rate has fallen from 4.5% to 3.75%, with treasury advisors forecasting further cuts to 3.5% by June 2026 and 3.25% by December 2026. The paper notes 10-year gilt yields have risen as high as 5.6% but remain volatile, reflecting fiscal concerns.
findings.matters: Sharp decline in investment income reduces resources available for council services without corresponding spending cuts, affecting financial flexibility and ability to self-fund capital plans.
findings.figures: Investment return: £1,914,000 (2025/26) to £1,100,000 (2026/27); Bank Rate: 4.5% to 3.75%; forecast to 3.5% by June 2026, 3.25% by December 2026
findings.quote: the expected investment return for 2026/27 has been calculated as £1,100,000. For comparison the investment return in 2025/26 is expected to be £1,914,000.

findings.headline: Council plans external borrowing for temporary accommodation properties during 2026/27.
findings.detail: Broadland is currently funding temporary accommodation purchases through internal borrowing from reserves, with external borrowing to replace this at an 'appropriate point in time'. The paper states further borrowing for additional properties 'is likely during 2026/27'. The actual timing of external borrowing has been delegated to the Assistant Director Finance in consultation with the Portfolio Holder for Finance.
findings.matters: New external debt increases council leverage and cost of capital; timing and scale of borrowing affect future interest rate exposure and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not disclosed in the strategy document
findings.quote: the purchase of temporary accommodation properties will initially be funded by internally borrowing from reserves, with this internal borrowing to be replaced by external borrowing at an appropriate point in time. Further borrowing to help purchase additional temporary accommodation properties, is likely during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: BDC Final Accounts 24-25 Audit Committee covering report
findings.headline: Revaluation loss of £2.6m on Thorpe Lodge asset held for sale
findings.detail: A revaluation loss of £2.6m on Thorpe Lodge (within Asset Held for Sale) was reclassified from the Revaluation Reserve to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement between draft and final accounts, contributing to the increase in total comprehensive income and expenditure from £709k surplus to £12.2m surplus.
findings.matters: Large asset revaluation losses can indicate property portfolio stress or market headwinds affecting the council's capital position.
findings.figures: £2.6m revaluation loss on Thorpe Lodge; total comprehensive income and expenditure increased from £709k to £12.2m surplus
findings.quote: This also included the reclassification of a revaluation loss on Thorpe Lodge (within Asset Held for Sale) from the Revaluation Reserve to the CIES of £2.6m.

findings.paper_title: BDC Final Accounts 24-25 Audit Committee covering report
findings.headline: Audit fee over £143,000 with expected additional fee variation, stretched finance team resources
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit fee will exceed £143,000, equating to over 143 days of audit work. EY submitted 219 individual information requests between March and December 2025, most containing multiple sub-requests. The auditors identified delays in obtaining valuation and actuarial reports and expect to raise a scale fee variation for audit delays.
findings.matters: Escalating audit costs and extended timelines consume finance team capacity and suggest audit complexity or control weaknesses that extend deadlines and increase costs beyond standard fees.
findings.figures: Audit fee over £143,000; 219 individual information requests March-December 2025; over 143 days of audit work estimated at £1,000/day
findings.quote: This year's audit fee will be over £143,000. Although it is not possible to know how many audit days this precisely equates to, if we assume a daily rate of c£1,000 this equates to over 143 days of audit work.

findings.paper_title: BDC Final Accounts 24-25 Audit Committee covering report
findings.headline: Material pension liability adjustment of £11.1m made between draft and final accounts
findings.detail: The pension scheme liability was adjusted by £11.127m following updated information from the pension fund and asset ceiling adjustments. This changed the net assets position from £66.696m to £78.213m. The timing mismatch (pension fund audit completed after draft accounts were published) requires annual re-estimation.
findings.matters: Large material adjustments to key liabilities between draft and final accounts indicate potential weaknesses in initial valuation processes or timing issues that could affect transparency and financial stability.
findings.figures: £11.127m pension scheme liability adjustment; net assets increased from £66.696m to £78.213m; pension reserve increased by £11.1m to £41.5m
findings.quote: Pension scheme liability adjustment following updated information from the pension fund and asset ceiling adjustments 11,127

findings.paper_title: BDC Final Accounts 24-25 Audit Committee covering report
findings.headline: Three consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions remain unresolved
findings.detail: Broadland has received disclaimed audit opinions on its 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts. The council is now presenting 2024/25 accounts with the audit still ongoing (the audit results report is included elsewhere on this agenda). Recovering from disclaimed opinions requires significant work over years, and the underlying capacity issues in the profession remain.
findings.matters: Unaudited accounts for multiple years represent a significant governance and transparency issue for lenders, with no certainty yet on whether 2024/25 will break the cycle.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24); backstop date for 2024/25 publication is 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Broadland District Council has received declaimed audit opinions on its 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 Accounts.

findings.paper_title: Broadland District Council - LG Draft Audit Results Report 24-25
findings.headline: Multiple errors in key working papers and procedures incomplete; short-term debtors and creditors insufficiently detailed for audit testing.
findings.detail: The auditor identified errors in key working papers including the Fixed Asset Register and payroll reconciliation. More significantly, key populations including short-term debtors and creditors were not sufficiently broken down to individual transactions, which prevented the auditor from completing planned procedures in these areas. The auditor expects to raise a scale fee variation for audit delays caused by quality of evidence issues.
findings.matters: Inability to complete planned audit procedures on debtors and creditors populations means balances were not fully tested. If key receivable and payable populations are not properly itemized, material errors could exist undetected.
findings.figures: Errors identified in Fixed Asset Register and payroll reconciliation; timeframes extended for testing due to quality issues.
findings.quote: Most working papers and supporting evidence were generally of a good standard, however we identified errors in a number of key working papers including the Fixed Asset Register and the payroll reconciliation, leading to additional audit procedures. In addition, key populations including short term debtors and creditors were not sufficiently broken down to individual transactions, which resulted in an inability to complete planned procedures in these areas.

findings.paper_title: Broadland District Council - LG Draft Audit Results Report 24-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation incomplete; no workings prepared for Council as lessor; auditor cannot quantify impact of omitted disclosures.
findings.detail: The Council failed to prepare any disclosures or workings for its role as lessor under IFRS 16. The auditor identified approximately 10 required adjustments to Note 13 Leases relating to incomplete and inconsistent IFRS16 disclosures. The absence of any lessor-related workings means the auditor cannot quantify the materiality of the missing disclosures on the financial statements.
findings.matters: Missing lessor implementation workings indicate incomplete accounting policy implementation. The auditor's inability to quantify impact suggests management may not have fully identified all lease assets and obligations, creating potential for unrecognized liabilities.
findings.figures: Approximately 10 required adjustments identified in Note 13 Leases; materiality of omitted disclosures unquantifiable.
findings.quote: No disclosures or workings in relation to the Council as lessor have been prepared therefore, we do not have any assurance in this area. In the absence of any workings, we are unable to quantify how material an impact the omitted disclosures would have on the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Broadland District Council - LG Draft Audit Results Report 24-25
findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register control deficiency; multiple errors found in sample of £21.054 million of assets; lease data not kept current.
findings.detail: The auditor identified a general control deficiency over the maintenance and review of the Fixed Asset Register. In a sample of 7 assets worth £21.054 million, the auditor found two errors in revaluation movements in the register and inconsistencies between disclosures and the register. A separate control deficiency was noted whereby lease agreements used in asset valuations were not kept up to date with latest rental payments, creating risk of valuation errors.
findings.matters: The Fixed Asset Register is the primary control over asset valuations. Control deficiencies indicate management oversight is weak, and material errors in the £27.0 million property asset base could go undetected.
findings.figures: Sample of 7 assets tested totalling £21.054 million; property, plant and equipment (including investment properties) valued at £27.0 million (prior year £24.2 million).
findings.quote: We identified a general control deficiency over the maintenance and review of the fixed asset register due to the volume of error identified, both from our procedures performed over land and building valuations, as well as wider procedures performed over property, plant and equipment; and We also identified a control deficiency whereby lease agreements used in the valuation for some assets were not always kept up to date with the latest rental payments, which could result in errors in the asset valuation.

findings.paper_title: Broadland District Council - LG Draft Audit Results Report 24-25
findings.headline: Pension fund liability jumped to £12.8 million from £1.35 million prior year, requiring £11.127 million correction; three versions of actuary report.
findings.detail: The Council's Local Government Pension Scheme deficit increased dramatically to £12.8 million at 31 March 2025 from £1.35 million prior year. Three different IAS19 reports were produced (May, September, October 2025) due to changes in pension fund valuations and illiquid private asset values. The Council incorrectly calculated the asset ceiling effect in 2023/24 and 2024/25 by incorrectly deducting an unfunded obligation of £0.773 million, and failed to disclose the ongoing Virgin Media court case affecting pension position.
findings.matters: A £11 million swing in pension liability represents a material deterioration in net asset backing. Multiple actuarial report iterations suggests either poor initial estimation or significant volatility in the underlying pension fund; either indicates uncertainty for lenders assessing long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Pension fund deficit £12.8 million (prior year £1.35 million); auditor identified £11.127 million correction; unfunded obligation of £0.773 million incorrectly deducted.
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025 this totalled £12.8 million (prior year £1.35 million). A further IAS19 report was obtained in October 2025 following an updated valuation of the pension fund's illiquid private assets, resulting in additional differences.

findings.paper_title: Broadland District Council - LG Draft Audit Results Report 24-25
findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements; third consecutive year without audit assurance on accounts.
findings.detail: The auditor disclaimed their opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. This follows disclaimers on 2022/23 and 2023/24, meaning the Council has no audit assurance on its accounts for three consecutive years. The auditor was unable to complete detailed audit procedures needed for an unmodified opinion due to the impact of prior year disclaimers on assurance over brought-forward balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion removes the primary control mechanism used by lenders to verify financial position and performance. Three years without audit assurance means the Council's reported financial position is unverified and unreliable for credit decisions.
findings.figures: Prior disclaimers issued 29 November 2024 (2023/24) and 20 February 2025 (2022/23); backstop date for 2024/25 audit was 27 February 2026.
findings.quote: Because of the significance of the matter described in the basis for disclaimer of opinion section of our report, we have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion on these financial statements.

findings.headline: Interest income forecast £55,610 below budget (3.6% variance) due to bank rate reductions from 4.5% to 4.0%
findings.detail: The council budgeted £1.55m in investment income for 2025/26 but is now forecasting £1.494m (£55.6k shortfall). Bank of England rate cuts in May (to 4.25%) and August (to 4.0%) have reduced returns on the council's £59.3m investment portfolio.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council's financial position is sensitive to interest rate movements. For a lender, this rate sensitivity is relevant when considering Broadland's exposure to future rate movements, particularly as the council is increasing borrowing for temporary accommodation.
findings.figures: £1,494,390 forecast vs £1,550,000 budgeted; £55,610 shortfall; bank rate cut from 4.50% to 4.00%; £59.262m investment portfolio
findings.quote: Interest received on external cash investments during the financial year is forecast to be around £1,494,390 which is £55,610 below the budget of £1,550,000.

findings.headline: Cabinet approved £3.4m capital budget for additional temporary accommodation in April 2025, funded 50% from borrowing, increasing Capital Financing Requirement four-fold
findings.detail: Cabinet approved a £3.4m capital budget for temporary accommodation in April 2025, funded 50% from borrowing (~£1.7m new debt), following earlier internal borrowing of £468k in 2024/25 for the same purpose. This drives the Capital Financing Requirement from £585k to £2.384m, and includes the impact of IFRS16 accounting changes. The council expects to remain within its £3m operational borrowing limit.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation expansion represents significant new capital commitment and debt issuance. Lenders need to understand this priority and whether rental income can service the debt. The strategy of deferring external borrowing until rates fall shows opportunistic debt management but is dependent on anticipated rate movements.
findings.figures: £3,412,600 capital budget, 50% funded from borrowing; £468,000 prior internal borrowing from 2024/25; CFR increased from £585,000 to £2,384,000
findings.quote: Cabinet on 22 April 2025 agreed to create a new capital budget of £3,412,600 to purchase additional temporary accommodation, and to fund 50% from borrowing.

findings.headline: Reserves of £35.4m will be materially consumed by capital programme and cannot address structural revenue deficit.
findings.detail: General revenue reserves of £11m plus earmarked reserves of £11m and capital grants of £13.1m total £35.4m. However, the council explicitly states that 'the Council has a significant capital programme which will call on a significant proportion of these Reserves over the next few years.' Reserves are being committed to capital, not available to absorb the revenue gap.
findings.matters: While starting reserves appear adequate in absolute terms, they are already committed to capital; a structural revenue deficit cannot be resolved through one-off reserve draws and indicates either future borrowing or service cuts are required.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves £35.4m: General Revenue £11m, Earmarked £11m, Capital Grants £13.1m
findings.quote: the Council has a significant capital programme which will call on a significant proportion of these Reserves over the next few years.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income projected to decline by £400k over MTFP period, reducing flexible revenue sources.
findings.detail: Investment income from treasury management modelled to fall from £1.55m in 2026/27 to £1.15m by 2030/31. This reduction in non-service revenue compounds the loss of government grants and further constrains council flexibility during a period of structural deficit.
findings.matters: Declining investment income alongside declining grants means the council loses flexibility precisely when it needs to absorb a growing budget gap; this increases risk that reserves must be drawn unsustainably.
findings.figures: Investment income: £1.55m (2026/27) declining to £1.15m (2030/31)
findings.quote: Investment Income - Treasury Mgt Reducing -1,550 -1,450 -1,350 -1,250 -1,150

findings.headline: Council faces structural annual budget gap growing from £210k to £504k by 2029/30, cumulative £1.8m shortfall.
findings.detail: Government funding changes since February 2025 (New Homes Bonus abolition, business rates pooling loss of £600k, EPR income down £408k, food waste grant removal) have materially worsened the position. Even with maximum permitted council tax increases, budget requirement exceeds funding each year. Officers have not yet identified sufficient savings to close the gap.
findings.matters: A structural revenue deficit of this scale, persisting across four years and growing each year, cannot be resolved through reserves alone and indicates either unplanned service cuts, unsustainable reserve depletion, or need for new borrowing.
findings.quote: Work has taken place to reduce the blue Budget Requirement line, but further work is still needed to bring the Budget Requirement and Funding into alignment.

findings.headline: Council borrowed £4.5m in May 2025 for Long Stratton By-pass infrastructure
findings.detail: The council arranged external borrowing of £4.5m in May 2025 for the Long Stratton By-pass infrastructure project. This adds to £20m borrowed in March 2022 for the capital programme. Total external borrowing now stands at £24.5m, within the £25m operational limit but at 98% utilisation.
findings.matters: Borrowing decisions are material to council finances and must be assessed against debt capacity and revenue serviceability. This represents a 22.5% increase in external borrowing within one year.
findings.figures: £4.5m borrowed May 2025; total external debt £24.5m; operational limit £25m (98% utilised); all borrowing has 10+ year maturity
findings.quote: And in May 2025 £4.5m was borrowed as part of the financing arrangements for the Long Stratton By-pass.

findings.headline: £10m bridging loan at Base Rate + 6% to fund St Giles housing phases indicates cashflow pressure
findings.detail: The new July 2025 credit facility includes a £10m temporary bridging loan to fund housing phases 10 and 16 at St Giles Park. Charged at Base Rate + 6%, this is the highest rate in the facility structure (compared to Base Rate + 2% for operational borrowing and Base Rate + 4% for amounts exceeding £20m). The need for this facility suggests the development is consuming cash faster than originally planned.
findings.matters: High-cost bridging finance at this scale signals the development may be experiencing cash pressures or unexpected acceleration. This affects the council's ability to recover the investment and refinance it on normal commercial terms.
findings.figures: £10m temporary bridging loan; Base Rate + 6% interest rate (with current base rate 4%, implying 10% total annual cost on this portion)
findings.quote: Interest on the daily balance of the temporary Bridging Loan (Additional £10,000,000 to cashflow the housing stock from phases 10 and 16 at St Giles Park) is charged at an annual rate of Base Rate + 6%.

findings.headline: Loans to Big Sky Developments increased by £8.3m to £27.76m in six months
findings.detail: The council's lending to Big Sky Developments Limited (for St Giles Park development) increased from £19.46m to £27.76m between March and September 2025. This represents 43% growth in a single quarter. The loans were novated into a new credit facility in July 2025, reflecting refinancing activity.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council's capital investments are on track and understand material exposures. This scale of increase in development lending in one quarter warrants scrutiny of project progress, cost control, and repayment risk.

news_drafts.headline: South Norfolk Council tax reduction costs rise 11% over two years as caseloads remain stable
news_drafts.lead: South Norfolk's share of Council Tax Reduction scheme costs has risen from £541,100 to £601,300 over two years, driven entirely by rising council tax levels rather than growing caseloads. The council has identified a constraint on its ability to reduce these costs: 98 to 99 per cent of working-age recipients receive Universal Credit, making them an extremely vulnerable population. The council's own papers state that cutting support "may not generate an equivalent increase in collectable Council Tax income and may instead increase hardship, debt and recovery costs". Any saving from reducing the scheme could be offset by higher collection losses and enforcement expenses. The committee noted the pattern of rising costs is expected to continue as council tax increases year on year.
